passage.text: "Regular coffee is so last week. I only drink NCB now." Tom tosses his hair, then examines his imaginary manicure.
I laugh. His accent is a mash-up of Valley girl and faux-Parisian, which is not at all how Ms. Bely actually talks. But given how I've described her, I can't blame him for thinking so.
Mom pours herself coffee. "What's NCB?"
"Nitro cold brew," I say, trying out the same accent my brother used. "It's divine."
"It's iced coffee charged up with nitrogen," Tom explains in his regular voice. "I tried it once. It's actually not bad."

But I'm not ready to drop the impersonation, partly because I can't remember the last time my brother and I joked around at the breakfast table. Plus, I'm pretty good at the accent. "I always grab one after hot yoga," I say. "The juxtaposition of hot and cool is so thought-provoking."
Mom frowns. "Ada, is she really that insufferable? I thought she was nice."
"Anyone can be nice." I shrug. "What's insufferable is her shallowness. Her 'problems.' Her…meaninglessness."
"Nobody's meaningless."
"I don't know about that. Anyway, I just can't take people seriously who never do anything."
"What does she do when you babysit?" Tom asks.
This is new and amazing—Tom's interest in my life. Maybe he finally understands that I'm not a goofy, empty-headed kid anymore. I've changed a lot since he's been at college.

"Yoga, salon, whatever," I tell him, sticking my nose up the way I imagine Ms. Bely does. "Oh, she also hides out in her quote, unquote 'studio.'" I lean in conspiratorially. "The boys call it the 'mommy-time room.'"
Tom snorts, and I grin. Not goofily, I don't think.
"Well, she provides you with a paycheck," Mom says, pointing to the clock. Whoops, my shift is from nine to one. I grab my keys. "See you guys when I return from the Posh Side."
"Good luck," Tom says.

Raindrops splatter on my windshield as I park; we'll have to stay inside today. I picture the three of us in the playroom, crafting and playing board games. This is a sweet summer gig, I have to admit.
Aiden throws his arms around my waist as if it's been a year instead of just a day. "I had a toaster paste for breakfast!" I gently brush the crumbs off my mini-me's cheek.
"Toaster pastry," says Tony, his brother. "Paste is for sticking. Like what Mommy uses for—"
"I know what paste is!"
"No, 'cause you said—"
"Paste, what a great idea!" I exclaim. "That's what we'll do today. How about we make flags for July Fourth?"
They look at me, interest piqued. I've gotten good at this.
Ms. Bely dashes down the stairs. Peach running shoes, black yoga pants, black-and-gray scoop-neck shirt artfully layered over a peach tank. "How are you, Ada?"
"Good, how about you?"
"Great! I'll be back in a couple of hours." She kisses the boys, leaving peach lipstick on their cheeks. "Have fun, kids."
"We're doing paste, Mommy," Aiden says importantly. Tony and I exchange a smile.
"Sounds cool!" Ms. Bely winks at me before she leaves. False eyelashes for the gym, wow.
In the playroom, we pull construction paper, scissors, and glue out of the crafts box. "Tony, honey, this glue is nearly out. Is there more somewhere?"

"Why don't you ask me?" says Aiden. "I know, too. Anyway, you said paste." Aiden has scrambled up the climbing ladder that's bolted to the wall; he's eye-level with me now. "Paste, Ada, right? Not glue."
"Same thing," Tony and I say together, which makes us both laugh. "Let's try the closet," Tony says, pulling my hand.
The closet is stacked with bins. I pull down the one labeled papermaking. Tony and I spend about ten minutes carefully sorting through the bin. It's full of old magazines and junk mail, but no glue.
"We make homemade paper from this," Tony says.
"Really? Wait, where's Aiden?"
Tony shrugs, and I sigh. Sometimes Aiden hides under his bed. "Come on, Tony, let's go find him."
But he's nowhere in his bedroom.
"Aiden!" I call, walking through the house. Then louder. "Aiden!"
"Aiden! It's not funny!" Tony yells.

Suddenly, I hear a crash from below us. I race downstairs, into Ms. Bely's studio, which is open for some reason, and—oh. There's Aiden, dragging a huge plastic bucket of "acrylic gloss varnish" across the studio floor.
"Got the paste," he pants.
"You're not supposed to be in here without Mommy," Tony says, skidding into the room. "Right, Ada?"
But I don't answer, because I'm staring at the gigantic painting on the easel. No, it's not a painting, it's a collage. "Your mom's an artist?" I ask.
"Uh-huh," they say together.
I step closer. A woman holds a gigantic hourglass, and the sand is falling out and piling up around her feet. It's beyond me.
"Ada, let's make the flags," says Aiden.
"Give me one minute," I answer. I breathe deeply and stare into the hourglass woman's eyes, knowing that as soon as I stop, I'll have to face myself.

passage.text: A throng of passengers got off at the Division Street stop, so Masha and Molly were finally able to sit.
"Ah, that's better," Molly said. "Now we can talk. Masha, come to the presentation tonight. Please. It's not a social thing. It's educational!"
The streetcar swayed, and Masha grabbed Molly's arm to steady herself. "I already told you," she said. "I can't."
"Can't!" Molly waved her hands as if batting away a fly. "Of course you can. No work tomorrow, remember? Relax for once! Do something fun."
"I am. Mama and I are baking rugelach." Seeing Molly's confused expression, Masha explained, "It's a dessert."
Molly waved her hand again. "Rosie can help her."
"Rosie!" Masha laughed.
"Why not? I bet you made roo-gla at her age."
"Rosie isn't interested. She's an American. And it's rugelach, not 'roo-gla.' You make it sound like a dance."

"See, now that would be fun." Molly deepened her voice. "Ladies and gentlemen! Presenting the roo-gla, the hottest dance of 1920!" She giggled. "Anyway, what are you even saying? You're American, too. You live here, don't you?"

"Yes, but Rosie is…of here." Masha's younger sister wore sailor-style blouses, owned a dozen ribbons for her bobbed hair, and knew all the latest songs. The heady aroma of yeast and nuts could never transport her back to their homeland, which Rosie barely remembered. As far as Rosie was concerned, America was their homeland. Whoops, Molly was talking.
"—just as American as she is. As American as apple pie! Come with me, Masha, and I'll bake an apple pie for your mama. You don't need roo-gla." Molly paused. "Ru-ge-lach."
Masha fell back against the seat, laughing. But then she sat up. "Wait a minute, Molly. Why are you so keen on this lecture?"

"I'm very interested in ancient art," Molly said. She tossed her copper curls and gazed at Masha with wide-eyed innocence. Masha stared back, eyes narrowed. Finally, Molly threw up her hands. "I overheard Stephen talking, and—"
"Aha! So Stephen will be there, will he?" Masha tossed her own hair in an imitation of Molly. "I'm very interested in ancient art," she squeaked.
They collapsed into laughter. "Okay, okay." Molly wiped her eyes. "Now will you come? Who knows, maybe you'll meet a young man!" She elbowed Masha. "Someone you can bake roo-gla for."
"Don't be silly. The last thing I want is to spend my life cooking for some old-world husband."
"See! You're more American than you think!"

It was true. If Masha ever returned to the old country, she wouldn't fit in. Nor, she realized suddenly, would she want to. And yet, she didn't want to wear a bob either. Or eat apple pie. She wanted rugelach. And borscht. And to sing the old folk songs to her children. If, that is, she remembered them by the time she had children. She rubbed her temples.
"What's wrong?" Molly asked.
"Do you remember Ireland?"
"Not much, no. Do you remember Poland?"
"Just fragments," Masha said. "I don't want to let go of them."
"Ah." There was understanding in Molly's eyes. "They're part of you, those fragments."

"Yes. Yes, exactly." Masha squeezed Molly's hand as the streetcar swayed again. Despite all their differences, Molly was the best friend Masha had ever had. Molly understood her. "Okay, Molly. I'll come with you," Masha said.
"Oh, Masha, thank you! And you know what, I bet you'll like it more than I do!"
Masha shook her head, already missing the smell of the rugelach dough. She wondered whether her mother would mind.
But Mama was thrilled. "Wonderful, Masha, you need to go out more!"
Rosie came running. "Masha, try my blue dress. And let me put some rouge on your cheeks. No, don't rub it off. Honestly!"
When Molly came by, she pretended to fall over. "Look who's modern now! Seriously, Masha, you're beautiful."
As they walked arm in arm up Unity Street, Masha did feel relaxed. Maybe it was a good thing, getting out sometimes.

When they stepped into the Alliance lobby, Masha gazed around in amazement. "Wait until you see the lecture room," Molly said, pulling her along. It was a classroom, really, but airy and beautifully lit. Masha and Molly took seats near the front, where Stephen was sitting. Molly waved to him, her eyes rounded in a perfect simulation of surprise.

"Welcome to Unity Street Alliance!" The lecturer smiled. "Tonight we'll discuss an art form called mosaic, which has flourished since ancient times." She paused. "I like to think of it as the art of fragments. Here is one of my own attempts, amateur though it may be." She held up a board on which varied bits of ceramic were arranged to form a cohesive design. Masha stared, hand on her heart.
After a few moments, the woman returned the board to her lectern. "Let's begin with the Roman Empire…"
Masha glanced at Molly, who was sitting up straight, cheeks flushed. Masha suspected that her own expression was similarly exuberant.

passage.text: A throng of passengers got off at the Division Street stop, so Masha and Molly were finally able to sit.
"Ah, that's better," Molly said. "Now we can talk. Masha, come to the presentation tonight. Please. It's not a social thing. It's educational!"
The streetcar swayed, and Masha grabbed Molly's arm to steady herself. "I already told you," she said. "I can't."
"Can't!" Molly waved her hands as if batting away a fly. "Of course you can. No work tomorrow, remember? Relax for once! Do something fun."
"I am. Mama and I are baking rugelach." Seeing Molly's confused expression, Masha explained, "It's a dessert."
Molly waved her hand again. "Rosie can help her."
"Rosie!" Masha laughed.
"Why not? I bet you made roo-gla at her age."
"Rosie isn't interested. She's an American. And it's rugelach, not 'roo-gla.' You make it sound like a dance."

"See, now that would be fun." Molly deepened her voice. "Ladies and gentlemen! Presenting the roo-gla, the hottest dance of 1920!" She giggled. "Anyway, what are you even saying? You're American, too. You live here, don't you?"

Whoops, Molly was talking.

Masha fell back against the seat, laughing. But then she sat up. "Wait a minute, Molly. Why are you so keen on this lecture?"

"Aha! So Stephen will be there, will he?" Masha tossed her own hair in an imitation of Molly. "I'm very interested in ancient art," she squeaked.
They collapsed into laughter. "Okay, okay." Molly wiped her eyes. "Now will you come? Who knows, maybe you'll meet a young man!" She elbowed Masha. "Someone you can bake roo-gla for."

passage.text: Mom looked up from the coffee pot. "You're going jogging in sandals?"
John grinned. "They're not sandals. They're Vips. For running on the beach."
"Referring to shoes by brand name is free advertising for companies," Dad interjected.

"Whatever. Anyway, Coach said to run in the surf five days a week while we're here. That's twenty runs. I didn't want to trash my sneakers." John raised his eyebrows at Dad. "I mean, my Crotes." Dad laughed and turned back to his reading. He was thumbing through a sheaf of neatly typewritten pages.
"Wait, Michael, is that a brief?" Mom stomped to the table and jerked the document out of Dad's hands. "The doctor said not to even think about work this month. That's why we're here, remember?"
"Thought it was for your marine research," John said, stretching his hamstrings.
"Both," huffed Mom. She looked from Dad to John, her face thoughtful. "Hey, Michael, maybe you should join—"
"No!" Dad and John said in unison.
"But you used to do stuff together all the time! Remember those obstacle courses you built?"
"Honey. That was years ago. Before he turned into a teenager."
"Yeah," said John, "and before he turned into Atticus Finch. Anyway, he'd slow me down."
Mom sighed and walked to the bookshelf, which the property manager had stuffed with books. She grabbed a thick volume and plunked it onto the table. "At least read something non-lawyerly."
As the door closed behind her, John picked up the book. "Cape Hatteras and the Lost Colony: The Unexamined Connection." He snorted. "Maybe you can read about alien sightings next."
"Have fun in your sandals," Dad muttered, pushing the book away.
But when John returned, Dad was staring at his computer, the book propped open beside it.
"The Lost Colony may have migrated here," he said.
"You're falling for it? They died, Dad. Starvation, disease, an attack, take your pick. But they didn't migrate."

"Except no one ever found the hundred and fifty dead bodies, did they? Here, listen to this." Dad read aloud from the screen: "'Modern archaeology may hold the key to the centuries-old mystery of the Lost Colony. Recently excavated artifacts suggest the colonists fled Roanoke for present-day Cape Hatteras, where they assimilated with the Croatoans.'"
John looked at Dad. "They seriously found artifacts?"
"Yep. Nothing conclusive, but interesting enough to raise the possibility."
"Wow."
"And guess what." Dad clicked the mouse. "There's a dig this Saturday. What luck, huh? I already registered us as volunteers."
"Wait, us?"
"Well," said Dad, "aren't you supposed to do a history project this summer? For that senior seminar you're all excited about?"
"Oh, yeah. Huh." John skimmed the screen over Dad's shoulder.
"I ordered us some Dares. They're steel-toed boots, but I refer to them by brand," Dad said.
John had to chuckle. He could already tell that Dad was getting way too obsessed.
But as it turned out, so were all the other volunteers. They clustered around the registration table, clutching wire mesh trays and chattering. The excitement was contagious.
John and Dad were assigned to an archaeology graduate student named Virginia. "First dig?" she asked.
They nodded.
"Well, don't worry. It's pretty basic." She demonstrated how to sort through the dirt. "Like gem mining," she said. "If you find something interesting, or even boring, call me over."

John and Dad got to work, sifting through mounds of dirt and rocks. Just as the novelty started to wear off, John spotted a small metallic object in his tray. He cleared away the dirt and dusted the object with his brush. Okay, it was definitely old. Definitely from a different time. Still, there was something familiar about it.
"I think it's one of those connectors. For fastening skirts and things," Dad said, leaning over John's shoulder.
John started. "Jeez, Dad! You trying to make me drop it?"
"Whoops, sorry." Together they crouched in silence, staring at the connector. "Croatoan clothing wouldn't have had these," Dad finally said.
John had been thinking the exact same thing. It reminded him of when he and Dad used to build stuff together; sometimes they hadn't even needed to talk.
"I know," he told Dad now. His heart was pounding. "Hook and eye," he said, finally remembering. "That's what they're called."
Dad waved Virginia over. John held his breath as she examined the hook. He couldn't believe this was happening.
"Really nice," Virginia said. "You're right, it's part of a hook and eye. We'll add it to the others."
"What?" Dad sounded incredulous. "You have more?"
"Oh, yes. They were quite common starting around the eighteenth century."
John and Dad looked at each other. "The Lost Colony disappeared in 1590," John muttered. Dad nodded.
"Well, yeah. But this is still a great find." Virginia placed the hook and eye in a plastic baggie. "Nice job, guys. Keep going!" She hurried away.
John and Dad stared after her in sheepish silence. Finally, Dad sighed. "Okay, that was…well. Let's call it a lesson in humility."
John sighed, too. "Seriously."
They laughed, then returned to sifting dirt.

passage.text: Knock, knock.

The child who lives in the trailer opposite my own is at my door. Her hair is so blonde, it's almost as white as mine, and it's jerked into a ponytail. Purple glasses. A darting, catlike quality to her movements. I remain, unconcerned, on the sofa with my book. She'll leave shortly, as she always does.
Knock, knock.

I suppose it's rude to ignore her like this, but in all likelihood, the child wants what I can't offer: a cliché. A comforting, grandmotherly type who bakes cookies and pats arms and…well, whatever else it is they do.
Knock, knock.
I realize I've read an entire paragraph without absorbing it. Irritated, I flick the page back.
Knock, knock, knock!

Now I slap my book down. The child wants a cliché? Fine. But she's not getting Grandma. She's getting Crone. I stride to the door, open it a crack, and scowl, expecting her to back off. Instead, she slinks through the sliver of open doorway. Did I mention she was catlike?
Catgirl stalks over to the sofa and settles herself there, placing her lavender backpack just so.
A voice calls, "Celia, I can't see you!"
"I don't need to be seen, Mother!" Catgirl's tone is indignant, like how cats would sound if they could speak.

"What do you mean, you don't need to be seen?" I snap. "You're nowhere near old enough for that luxury." I yank the door wide so that Catgirl's mother, standing in her own doorway, can see straight through to my couch. That's how close together these trailers are.

I expect the mother to say something like, "Catgirl, you come home this instant!" But she just appraises me, nods, and shuts her door. My mouth is literally hanging open at this point. What does the woman think I am, a free babysitter?

Folding my arms, I turn back to the scene in my living room. Catgirl, now clutching a notepad and pencil, gazes at me through her ludicrous eyewear. "I have a few questions," she snips, all Associated Press.
"Excuse me?"
"May I ask you a few questions, please."
"What is this, some sort of school project?"
She blinks. "Yes. Exactly. A history project."
Great. I'm history.
But five minutes of humoring her is certainly a fair price to pay for permanent privacy, so I lay down my terms. "After this? That's it. No more banging on my door. No impromptu visits. Agreed?"
Catgirl nods curtly and taps her pencil on the notepad, like she has nine other interviews to rush off to.
"Fine," I say. "Proceed."
She pounces. "What was your former identity?"
"Excuse me?"
"Let me rephrase. Who were you before the war?"
"What war?"
She squints at me like I'm under a microscope. "I think you know," she purrs. She pulls a book out of her backpack and presents it with a flourish. Spies of World War II: Hiding in Plain Sight.

Wow. Guess I was wrong about the Grandma cliché. I start laughing so hard that I have to put my hand on the kitchen table to steady myself. And I realize it's been a long time since I laughed. And then I remember that it's July. No school, no homework. No projects.
Poor Catgirl sits on my couch and watches me with a dismayed face, the ridiculous book sliding off her lap. Catgirl the spy. Thinking she's caught a fellow spy.

"I was a baby during World War II," I chortle. "How old do you imagine I am?" Catgirl looks confused at the thought that I was ever a baby. She opens her mouth, but I'm on a roll. "Before you investigate your next case," I start, putting "case" in air quotes, "you might want to bone up on common sense."

Catgirl's eyes fill—oh, criminy—and I drop my hands. She reaches for her backpack, but it topples, spilling notepads, pencils, and another book onto the floor. The Loneliness One Dare Not Sound: The Life of Emily Dickinson. Wait, Dickinson?

I watch her shoving everything back into the backpack, and now it's like I'm the one looking through the microscope. And I see her as she must actually be: a quirky, intelligent girl with a hopeless glut of imagination, stuck in a relentlessly lonely summer and creating a whole scenario about the odd old woman across the way. A woman who does, let's face it, have a past she wants to leave in the past. Celia wasn't all wrong.
I sigh, then walk over and sit on the other end of the sofa. "Okay, look," I say. "I'm sorry I laughed."
"Whatever," Celia mutters.
We lapse into silence, the emptiness of summer stretching in front of us.

passage.text: As he parks, my father says, "Leah. About Madison. She's not exactly…herself."
I busy myself with the door handle. "Yeah. I mean, hard place to be. The hospital."
"And also, when she comes home. The adjusting."
"Right."
My father and I both tend to speak in staccato when we're nervous.
We walk toward the medical center, and I consider his phrasing: "Not exactly herself." I wonder if she even cares. Maybe she's happy to cast off her old self. To molt.

Like that time at the Turvy Street Festival. We'd gone together, just the two of us. Booths full of pottery and batik and beaded jewelry. The smell of sugar and grease. We had just split a funnel cake, and Madison had gone to throw away the plate. She came running back. "Leah, there's a free haircut booth!"

"Nothing's free," I said. She laughed, grabbed my hand, and pointed to a plastic banner: Free Cuts from À L'envers Salon! The bouncing hairdresser spied us immediately and cried, "Ladies! Let Pierre transform you!"

"Let's go," I muttered, but Madison was already jumping into the chair and requesting "something radical." Pierre's scissors flashed; his razor whirred. The two of them chatted like soul mates. Fifteen minutes later, he triumphantly spun her chair around to face the mirror. She stared at her reflection. "I'm gone," she breathed. I shuddered, but Not-Madison didn't notice. She flung her arms around Pierre, then plopped a ten-dollar tip into his hand. The last of her money.
Now I shudder again, and my father touches my shoulder. "I mean, why would she have thought it was a good idea to—" I cut myself off.
My father says, "This might not be the best time—"
"I know. Forget it."
And suddenly, we're in the lobby, the elevators yawning open.
I stop walking. "We should get a coffee," I say. "For Mom. Shouldn't we?"
Dad nods. "All right." We turn from the elevators.

The cafeteria: salads in cellophane, fries wilting under heat lamps, aluminum vats of coffee. Dad and I deliberate over caffeine, sweetener, dairy. There are two lines for the cashier, one on either side of her. She takes turns so that the lines will stay even, but they aren't. I make sure we join the longer one, my father holding one cup of regular and one cup of decaf, me clutching packets of sugar, sweetener, creamer. So many choices.

"Just choose!" I can hear Madison saying. And I remember plastic yellow ducks floating in a tub of greasy water, state fair music, my parents laughing. Ten years ago? Twelve? We were playing one of those rigged carnival games—the one where you get to catch a duck with a fishing pole, then exchange it for a prize.

Madison caught her duck within three seconds. The barker unhooked it, flicked his eyes over the label on the bottom, and shouted, "Goldilocks here just won herself a spider ring!" Madison was so proud of that ring, twisting it around her index finger and grinning. But I didn't want a dud prize. I wanted the plushy purple dog that no one ever won. I stared at the revolving ducks. One of them was right, but which? My hands were sweating as I gripped the pole. Did I ever even choose? I don't remember. I only remember Madison jumping up and down, yelling, "Choose! Choose! Leah, just choose!"

The elevator dings, and my father and I step out, carefully balancing our coffee suite. We walk down the hall, past the nurses' station, past closed door after closed door, until finally my father stops at Madison's.
"Dad," I say.
He turns.
"I need the restroom. Here." I dump the creamers and sweeteners into his jacket pocket. I don't even open the door for him.

The restroom: banging doors, mirrors under unforgiving lights. I stare at the circles under my eyes. I could text him: Not feeling well. Will wait for you in lobby, no, in front of hospital, no, in parking garage, no, in the closet at home.

I found Madison there once, in the coat closet by the living room. About five years ago. It was the day she brought Impulse home—mangy, scrawny, abandoned. I opened the closet to hang my jacket, and there she was, arms around him as he trembled.
I screamed, and Impulse barked. Madison shushed me.
"Cutie needs darkness and quiet," she murmured. "Come in." But I didn't. I just closed the door, remembering that I had seen him, too, just the day before, skulking in the bushes.
Impulse—or Cutie, as only Madison calls him—has been hiding under her bed for the past two days. I still don't know how to help him.

I wash my hands, slowly dry them on rough paper towels. Finally, I leave the restroom, stand in the hall. The elevators are ahead, Madison's room off to my right. And I close my eyes against the burden of choice.

"Nothing's free," I said. She laughed, grabbed my hand, and pointed to a plastic banner: Free Cuts from À L'envers Salon! The bouncing hairdresser spied us immediately and cried, "Ladies! Let Pierre transform you!"

"Let's go," I muttered, but Madison was already jumping into the chair and requesting "something radical." Pierre's scissors flashed; his razor whirred. The two of them chatted like soul mates. Fifteen minutes later, he triumphantly spun her chair around to face the mirror. She stared at her reflection. "I'm gone," she breathed. I shuddered, but Not-Madison didn't notice. She flung her arms around Pierre, then plopped a ten-dollar tip into his hand. The last of her money.
Now I shudder again, and my father touches my shoulder. "I mean, why would she have thought it was a good idea to—" I cut myself off.
My father says, "This might not be the best time—"
"I know. Forget it."
And suddenly, we're in the lobby, the elevators yawning open.
I stop walking. "We should get a coffee," I say. "For Mom. Shouldn't we?"
Dad nods. "All right." We turn from the elevators.

The cafeteria: salads in cellophane, fries wilting under heat lamps, aluminum vats of coffee. Dad and I deliberate over caffeine, sweetener, dairy. There are two lines for the cashier, one on either side of her. She takes turns so that the lines will stay even, but they aren't. I make sure we join the longer one, my father holding one cup of regular and one cup of decaf, me clutching packets of sugar, sweetener, creamer. So many choices.

"Just choose!" I can hear Madison saying. And I remember plastic yellow ducks floating in a tub of greasy water, state fair music, my parents laughing. Ten years ago? Twelve? We were playing one of those rigged carnival games—the one where you get to catch a duck with a fishing pole, then exchange it for a prize.

Madison caught her duck within three seconds. The barker unhooked it, flicked his eyes over the label on the bottom, and shouted, "Goldilocks here just won herself a spider ring!" Madison was so proud of that ring, twisting it around her index finger and grinning. But I didn't want a dud prize. I wanted the plushy purple dog that no one ever won. I stared at the revolving ducks. One of them was right, but which? My hands were sweating as I gripped the pole. Did I ever even choose? I don't remember. I only remember Madison jumping up and down, yelling, "Choose! Choose! Leah, just choose!"

The elevator dings, and my father and I step out, carefully balancing our coffee suite. We walk down the hall, past the nurses' station, past closed door after closed door, until finally my father stops at Madison's.
"Dad," I say.
He turns.
"I need the restroom. Here." I dump the creamers and sweeteners into his jacket pocket. I don't even open the door for him.

The restroom: banging doors, mirrors under unforgiving lights. I stare at the circles under my eyes. I could text him: Not feeling well. Will wait for you in lobby, no, in front of hospital, no, in parking garage, no, in the closet at home.

I found Madison there once, in the coat closet by the living room. About five years ago. It was the day she brought Impulse home—mangy, scrawny, abandoned. I opened the closet to hang my jacket, and there she was, arms around him as he trembled.
I screamed, and Impulse barked. Madison shushed me.
"Cutie needs darkness and quiet," she murmured. "Come in." But I didn't. I just closed the door, remembering that I had seen him, too, just the day before, skulking in the bushes.
Impulse—or Cutie, as only Madison calls him—has been hiding under her bed for the past two days. I still don't know how to help him.

I wash my hands, slowly dry them on rough paper towels. Finally, I leave the restroom, stand in the hall. The elevators are ahead, Madison's room off to my right. And I close my eyes against the burden of choice.

header.text: <instructions>Consider this claim:</instructions>

contents.text: People should be rewarded for winning, not merely participating.
<instructions>Which is the strongest evidence to support the claim?</instructions>

choices.text: On giving out participation trophies, parenting blogger Allison Slater Tate writes, "There is something to teaching kids that it is worth keeping a commitment, that we value this. Winning and losing is not a lesson that kids need to search out to find. It's everywhere."
Pittsburgh Steelers linebacker James Harrison took away his children's participation trophies, posting on Instagram that he wouldn't give them back until his sons earned real trophies by winning.

Chris Hudson, founder of the website Understanding Teenagers, warns, "Ironically, participation medals don't build confidence, but they do create entitlement. Confidence and resilience don't come from false praise or rewarding normal behavior."
